power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: An a priori power analysis was conducted for the primary confirmatory hypothesis (H1), the within-person (Level 1) association between daily exposure to thin and sexualised female bodies on TikTok (in seconds) and subsequent state body satisfaction. Given the hierarchical structure of the data, with repeated end-of-day EMA observations (Level 1) nested within participants (Level 2), a multilevel modelling approach that explicitly accounts for this dependency was required. Based on the information available at the preregistration stage, an analytic sample of approximately 68 female participants was anticipated, each contributing on average 10 valid end-of-day EMA assessments across the two-week study period.
table.header: Power analysis

table.text: To inform the expected effect size, we drew on the experimental literature on exposure to appearance-ideal content. In a meta-analysis of experimental studies, de Valle et al. 44 found that on the between-person level viewing appearance-ideal images on social media had an immediate, moderate negative effect on body image on the between person level relative to both non-appearance control content (Hedges' g = -0.61) and other appearance-related images (Hedges' g = -0.68). Following Arend and Schäfer, 49 moderate Level 1 direct effect was treated as corresponding to approximately 9% explained outcome variance at Level 1. Consistent with current best practice for power analysis in intensive longitudinal designs, power considerations were informed by the Monte Carlo simulation study of Arend and Schäfer 49 for two-level models. Based on the anticipated sample size and number of repeated assessments, the planned study was expected to be adequately powered to detect a moderate within-person association between daily appearance content exposure and state body satisfaction at the subsequent EMA assessment. No corresponding a priori power analysis was preregistered for the beauty-filter or beauty-label extensions.

table.title: Investigating the relationship between exposure to thin and sexualised female bodies on TikTok and body satisfaction among female adolescents
table.research_questions:
Is higher exposure to thin and sexualised female bodies on TikTok linked to lower body satisfaction in female adolescents? Hypothesis 1 (within-person level): The daily time (in seconds) female adolescents spend watching TikTok videos containing at least one thin and sexualised female body (indexed by slim body stature and minimal clothing) will predict subsequent lower end-of-day body satisfaction.

Exploratory hypothesis 1 (within-person level): Lower start-of-day body satisfaction will predict female adolescents spending more daily time (in seconds) watching TikTok videos containing at least one thin (indexed by slim body stature) and sexualised female body (indexed by minimal clothing and sexually suggestive posing of body or face).

Exploratory hypothesis 2 (between-person level): Female adolescents spending more daily time (in seconds) – on average – watching TikTok videos containing at least one thin (indexed by slim body stature) and sexualised female body (indexed by minimal clothing and sexually suggestive posing of body or face) will report lower average end-of-day body satisfaction. 

Exploratory hypothesis 3 (between-person level): Female adolescents with lower average start-of-day body satisfaction will spend more daily time (in seconds) – on average – watching TikTok videos containing at least one thin (indexed by slim body stature) and sexualised female body (indexed by minimal clothing and sexually suggestive posing of body or face).
table.datasets_used:
We will use data collected from 13–18-year-olds across six schools in Cambridgeshire, Birmingham and Manchester. Of the full study sample, 120 participants provided TikTok data and took part in the EMA study, which involved completing three daily assessments over a two-week period in 2024 (see Yap et al., 2024, for details).

Among those initially recruited, 55.71% were female (all cisgender; no transgender participants). During the 14-day EMA period, participants received 42 prompts (three per day). Completeness checks (see the ‘Data Access’ section of Yap et al., 2024) indicated an average response rate of 74%, equating to approximately 31 completed assessments per participant.
Therefore, we anticipate that the subset of data we intend to use will comprise 67 participants, each of whom will have an average of 31 EMA observations.

table.measured_variables:
State body satisfaction:
•	Single item measurement 3 times a day over a period of 14 days through ecological momentary assessment (EMA); will be treated as continuous
•	Instruction: ‘Carefully read the following statements and select the option that best reflects the way you have felt since the last notification.
•	Item taken from the State Self-Esteem Scale (SSES; Heatherton & Polivy, 1991): ‘I felt satisfied with the way my body looks’
•	Response options (5-point-scale): 1= not at all, 2=a little bit, 3=somewhat, 4=very much, 5=extremely) 


Daily exposure time (in seconds) viewing content featuring at least one thin and sexualised female body: 


1. Video coding strategy:

Segmentation: Videos are first segmented into one or more still images (“video stills”) at a rate of one frame per second. As sampling begins at 0 seconds, the total number of stills equals the video’s duration in seconds plus one.

Exclusion of unviewed stills: From the resulting pool of stills, we will exclude stills captured from videos known to be unviewed – i.e., portions after the viewer started another video before the current one ended. If a video is the last in a viewing episode, we will assume it was watched in full (per viewing timestamps). All subsequent processing uses only the resulting subset of stills.

Content extraction pipeline: The remaining stills are then reduced stepwise at each stage of the pipeline, with each additional classification step minimizing noise in the stills pool and improving the feasibility of manual accuracy checks.

- Step 1 – human-presence filter: Retain only stills that clearly contain a person – i.e., a visible face, parts of the torso, or the thighs. Stills showing only minor body parts (e.g., just a hand within a landscape) are treated as no human present and removed from the pool.

- Step 2 – female-presence filter. Further narrow the pool to stills that depict a female-presenting person. Accept stills with a clear view of the face and/or torso or thighs. We will remove ambiguous cases where sex cannot be reliably assessed and retain only clear matches for further processing.

- Step 3 – thin female-presence filter: The pool is further narrowed to stills that (a) depict a female-presenting person who (b) shows a thin body build (i.e., minimal visible body fat). Ambiguous cases – where either the gender presentation of a thin individual cannot be reliably determined or the thin body build of a female-presenting person is indiscernible (e.g., face-only stills) – will be removed. Only clear matches are retained for the subsequent analysis pool.

- Step 4 – thin, sexualised female-presence filter. From the remaining pool, retain only stills that (a) depict a thin (minimal body fat), female-presenting individual and (b) present the subject in a sexualized manner – operationalized as minimal/ tight clothing (e.g., swimwear, lingerie, tight sportswear) and sexually suggestive posing of body or face (e.g., pouting lips). All other stills are removed.

Notes: The pipeline development process will include frequent checks throughout. Once the pipeline is finalised, each of the four steps will be manually validated using at least 1,000 randomly selected stills per content-classification step, evaluated by two independent reviewers who were not involved in pipeline development. If performance falls below 95% accuracy, we will iterate –refining prompts, tuning model hyperparameters, or adjusting decision thresholds, as appropriate – until we achieve at least 95% accuracy.
We will report accuracy and error rates, and adjust thresholds and model prompts as needed. Steps 1–3 will use openly available AI models. For Step 4, we will fine-tune a vision classifier using a training set derived from previously rated social-media images. We will train for a fixed number of epochs, select the best model by macro-F1 on a held-out set, and report full metrics and confusion matrices. 


2. Definitions and timing

Total exposure time (seconds). Count the number of viewed 1-second stills that are classified as containing at least one thin, sexualized female body. A participant’s total exposure time for a given day equals the number of qualifying 1-second stills within that day’s time window. To account for late bedtimes, we define a “day” as between 04:00 on a calendar day to 03:59 the following day. 

EMA scheduling. At intake, participants reported their typical availability for early morning, noon/afternoon, and evening. EMA invitations were scheduled accordingly:

table.missing_data_handling:
We will implement different strategies for the outcomes exposure to thin, sexualised female bodies and body satisfaction. 

Outcome daily exposure time (in seconds) viewing content featuring at least one thin and sexualised female body (exploratory hypotheses 1and 3):

We expect the following types of missing data:
- If participants did not use TikTok on a given day, they will be coded as having had no content exposure.
- If participants did use TikTok on a given day but some of the TikTok videos that users have viewed are not available (e.g., because they were deleted), we will assign each missed 1-second video still the average probability of seeing a thin and sexualised body of the other available videos stills on a given day.
- If participants did use TikTok on a given day but no TikTok videos are available, we will assign each missed video with the average probability of seeing a thin and sexualised body of the other available videos across the whole 14-day study period.



Outcome state body satisfaction – (hypothesis 1 + exploratory hypothesis 2):

We expect the following types of missing data:
- Participants did not fill in the EMA at the start/ end of a given day
- Participants filled in the EMA but skipped the state body satisfaction item.
In both cases, we will use multiple imputation to account for missing data and run analyses on the pooled imputations. 

Values will therefore be imputed based on the following model:

Hypothesis 1:
End-of-day body satisfaction ~ all other EMA variables at the most recent EMA occasion [overview provided in the codebook section] + 
                                                       [baseline measures:]
                                                       total score - Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire/ SDQ +
                                                       total score - Online andOffline Social Sensitivity Scale/ O2S3 +
                                                       total score - Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale/ IUS-C +
                                                       age + gender + house income +
                                                       ( 1 | participant)

Exploratory hypothesis 2
Start-of-day body satisfaction ~ all other EMA variables at the most recent EMA occasion [overview provided in the codebook section] + 
                                                         [baseline measures:]

                                                         total score - Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale/ IUS-C +

                                                         ( 1 | participant)


Imputation engine and settings: We will run multiple imputation in R with the ‘mitml’ package using ‘pan’ as the engine. Following recommended practice (e.g., Grund et al., 2018) and similar to de Haan et al. (2024), we will use a burn-in of 6,000 iterations, then draw m = 30 imputed datasets, each 200 iterations apart. Following recommended practice (Grund, Lüdtke, & Robitzsch, 2016, 2018) person-mean centering will be performed within each imputed dataset after imputation.

Diagnostics and sensitivity: We will inspect trace plots, the fraction of missing information, and within- vs. between-imputation variance to assess quality. If diagnostics indicate problems (e.g., poor convergence or very high fraction of missing information), we will increase m and/or the number of iterations and document any changes. For body satisfaction imputation model, we will repeat respective analyses with complete cases only as a sensitivity check and compare the results to those from the multiply imputed data.

table.effect_size: Sexualised images and videos featuring women who conform to thin beauty ideals have been shown in experimental studies to harm body image (de Valle et al., 2021). More specifically, de Valle et al. (2021) found in their meta-analysis that viewing appearance-ideal images on social media has an immediate, moderate negative impact on body image compared to (1) non-appearance control content (Hedges’ g = −0.61); and (2) other appearance-related images (Hedges’ g = −0.68). For hypothesis 1 the effects of interest relate to the direct effect of the level 1 predictor variable (daily exposure time [in seconds] viewing content featuring at least one thin and sexualised female body ) on the level 1 outcome variance in state body satisfaction. Following Arend and Schäfer (2019), a moderate level-1 direct effect explains 9% of the outcome variance.
table.statistical_power:
The present study is powered for the hypothesis 1. Based on the information provided in the ‘Dataset used’ section, we expect the data subset that we plan to use to include ~68 female participants, each of whom will have an average of ~31 EMA observations (three prompts per day over two weeks). Extrapolating from the overall response rate to the end-of-day EMA response rate, we assume that participants will have completed on average 10 end-of-day EMAs. As the data has a hierarchical structure, with end-of-day EMA observations (level 1) nested within individuals (level 2), a multilevel approach that accounts for this structure is required.
Daily-life assessments are nested within participants over time. Following best practices for power analysis in longitudinal daily-life studies with nested data, we base our power analysis on a comprehensive simulation study on two-level multilevel models which has been conducted by Arend and Schäfer (2019). Their simulation study suggests that the present study is powered to detect a moderate effect of the predictor daily exposure time (in seconds) viewing content featuring at least one thin and sexualised female body on state body satisfaction at the following EMA prompt.
table.inference_criteria: We will examine fixed effects estimates, statistical significance, their confidence intervals, random effects, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), as well as explained variance. table.title: Beauty Filters, Beauty content, and Body Satisfaction: An Ecological Momentary Assessment and Data-Donation Study Using TikTok Metadata in Adolescents
table.research_questions:
Is higher exposure to TikTok beauty content linked to lower body satisfaction in female adolescents? Primary hypothesis:

Hypothesis 1 (within-person level). More daily time (in seconds) that female adolescents spend watching TikTok videos containing a beauty filter will predict subsequent lower end-of-day body satisfaction.

Secondary hypotheses:

Hypothesis 2 (within-person level). More daily time (in seconds) that female adolescents spend viewing TikTok videos labeled as beauty content will predict subsequent lower end-of-day body satisfaction.

Hypothesis 3 (within-person level). Lower start-of-day body satisfaction will predict female adolescents spending more daily time (in seconds) watching TikTok videos with a beauty filter on that day.

Hypothesis 4 (within-person level). Lower start-of-day body satisfaction will predict female adolescents spending more daily time (in seconds) watching TikTok videos labelled as containing beauty content on that day.

Hypothesis 5 (between-person level). Female adolescents who spend more daily time (in seconds) – on average – watching TikTok videos tagged as using a beauty filter will report lower average end-of-day body satisfaction.

Hypothesis 6 (between-person level). Female adolescents who spend more daily time (in seconds) – on average – watching TikTok videos containing beauty content labels will report lower average end-of-day body satisfaction.
table.datasets_used:
The present study uses data collected from N = 358 adolescents aged 13–18 years recruited from six schools in Cambridgeshire, Birmingham, and Manchester (Yap et al., 2024). Of the full sample, 55.71% identified as female (all cisgender). A subsample of 119 participants provided TikTok data donation files and participated in the EMA component of the study, which involved completing three assessments per day over a two-week period in 2024.

Of the subsample, there were a total of 68 female adolescents. Two participants were subsequently excluded because the TikTok data they donated covered a period preceding the participation in the EMA study and therefore did not overlap with the EMA assessment window, precluding the derivation of time-varying exposure measures. The final analytic sample comprised N = 66 female adolescents.

State body satisfaction:
Single item measurement 3 times a day (morning, midday, evening) over a period of 14 days through ecological momentary assessment (EMA); will be treated as continuous
Instruction: ‘Carefully read the following statements and select the option that best reflects the way you have felt since the last notification.
Item taken from the State Self-Esteem Scale (SSES; Heatherton & Polivy, 1991): ‘I felt satisfied with the way my body looks’
Response options (5-point-scale): 1= not at all, 2=a little bit, 3=somewhat, 4=very much, 5=extremely)

1. Metadata extraction strategy

For each video in a participant's TikTok watch history, corresponding video metadata were obtained.

Beauty-filter classification: A video is classified as “beauty-filtered” if its metadata indicates use of at least one effect from the reference list below. We have constructed an a priori reference list of TikTok sticker effects that meet a working definition of “beauty filter”. On TikTok, a sticker effect is an augmented reality (AR) effect that users can apply to videos to modify or augment their appearance or surroundings. Beauty filters are defined as sticker effects that alter a user's facial or body appearance to conform more closely to idealized beauty standards, including changes such as skin smoothing, facial reshaping, makeup application, eye enlargement, lip enhancement, hair modification, or other cosmetic enhancements. This definition is consistent with prior experimental work examining beautifying and slimming filters (Schroeder & Behm-Morawitz, 2024).

To develop the reference list, we systematically identified candidate beauty filters using two complementary approaches. First, we labeled beauty filters based on their names having appearance-related keywords (e.g., “makeup”, “smooth”, “lipstick”, “lashes”, etc.). Second, MZ manually examined the 300 most frequently observed sticker effects in our dataset to identify additional appearance-altering effects that may not be captured through keyword labeling (e.g. “prettiest”, “cutest”). 

Beauty content classification: A video was classified as beauty-related if it carried one or more of TikTok's official content diversification labels associated with beauty content. These platform-generated labels are assigned by TikTok and are presumed to be derived from multiple features of the video, such as its transcript, caption, and visual content. Each video could receive multiple labels. To identify the set of beauty-related labels, we used snowball sampling beginning with three seed labels: "Beauty," "Beauty and Style," and "Beauty and Care." We then identified all labels that co-occurred with these seeds, yielding three additional unique labels: "Outfit," "Nail Art," and "Hair." Accordingly, we defined beauty-related content as videos containing any of these six labels, which collectively accounted for approximately 12.0% (48,202 of 403,046) of all videos watched by eligible female participants.

2. Definitions and timing

Video watch duration estimation: For each video, we have the participant's start time of viewing but not a stop time, so watch duration must be inferred. We first construct gaps for each video, which is the time elapsed between when a participant starts watching one video and when they start the next. Because a gap can span time spent off the app, we adjust it based on session context (a session being a continuous block of active in-app usage): if the next video falls within the same session, the gap is the raw time between events; if the session ends before the next video starts, the gap is capped at the session's own end time, excluding the off-app interval; if no session covering the event exists to verify either case, the raw gap is retained but flagged as unverified; and if there is no next event at all recorded for that participant, the gap is left unbounded.

Then, we cross-check the gap with the video length. Where the video's own length is known (from the downloaded file), watch duration is defined as the shorter of the video's length and the session-aware gap. If the gap is shorter, it means the participant navigated away before the video finished, so the gap itself is the true watch time; if the gap is longer than the video's length (including an unbounded gap), there was enough time for the video to have played out fully, so we assume it did and count the full video length.

Where the video's own length is unknown, there is no independent value to check the gap against, so the gap itself must serve as the watch-time estimate. We accept it only after a trust check, applied in decreasing order of confidence: (1) if the following event is confirmed within the same session, the participant was continuously active in the app throughout, so the raw gap is used directly; (2) failing that, if a session log is available and shows the session ended before the next video started, only the time up to that session's recorded end is used, since that is the portion known to reflect active viewing; (3) failing that, the raw gap is accepted only if it does not exceed the participant's own median duration across their trusted videos, defined as videos with a known length whose next event was also confirmed within the same session, as a plausibility check in the absence of any session data; (4) if none of these conditions hold, including the case of no following event at all, we substitute a random draw from that same trusted distribution (the participant's own length-known, session-confirmed videos), rather than assuming the video was watched in full or leaving the duration unbounded.

Exposure calculation: Total exposure per day is defined as the sum of watch durations (in seconds) across all videos classified as containing at least one beauty filter or a beauty-related content diversification label for that day. This sum is restricted to videos watched between 4:00am and the moment of the end-of-day assessment on that day.

3. EMA Response

EMA scheduling: At intake, participants reported their typical availability for early morning, noon/afternoon, and evening. EMA invitations were scheduled accordingly: 
Morning EMA: within the 2-hour window before school/work start time (e.g., if school starts at 08:30, the invitation is sent between 06:30–08:30). We classify this as ‘start-of-day’.
Afternoon EMA: within the 2-hour window after school/work ends. 
Evening EMA: within the 2-hour window before the participant’s reported bedtime. After an EMA invitation is sent, participants have 3 hours to complete the survey. We classify this as ‘end-of-day’.

table.missing_data_handling:
We will implement different strategies for the outcomes of exposure to beauty filters and beauty-related content and body satisfaction. 

Outcome daily exposure time (in seconds):

We expect the following types of missing data:
- If participants did not use TikTok on a given day, they will be coded as having had no content exposure (0 seconds) for that day.
- If participants used TikTok but some viewed videos are unavailable in the donation export (e.g., deleted), we will assign each missing video the average probability of beauty-filter (or beauty-label) status among the participant's other available videos for that day.
- If no videos are available for a given day despite TikTok use, we will assign the average probability of beauty-filter (or beauty-label) status from the participant's other available videos across the full 14-day period.
- If a participant's TikTok donation covers only some of the dates overlapping the 14-day EMA period rather than all of them, we will assign the average probability of beauty-filter (or beauty-label) status from the participant's other available videos across the full 14-day period for the non-overlapping EMA days.

Outcome state body satisfaction:

We expect the following types of missing data:
- Participants did not fill in the EMA at the start/ end of a given day
- Participants filled in the EMA but skipped the state body satisfaction item.
In both cases, we will use multiple imputation to account for missing data and run analyses on the pooled imputations. 

Values will therefore be imputed based on the following model:

End-of-day body satisfaction ~ all EMA variables at the most recent EMA occasion [overview provided in the codebook section] + seconds of beauty filter content consumed on that day + seconds of beauty labeled content consumed on that day
                                                       [baseline measures:]
                                                       total score - Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire/ SDQ +
                                                       total score - Online andOffline Social Sensitivity Scale/ O2S3 +
                                                       total score - Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale/ IUS-C +
                                                       age + house income +
                                                       ( 1 | participant)

Start-of-day body satisfaction ~ all EMA variables at the most recent EMA occasion [overview provided in the codebook section] + seconds of beauty filter content consumed the previous day + seconds of beauty labeled content consumed the previous day
                                                       [baseline measures:]
                                                       total score - Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire/ SDQ +
                                                       total score - Online andOffline Social Sensitivity Scale/ O2S3 +
                                                       total score - Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale/ IUS-C +
                                                       age + house income +
                                                       ( 1 | participant)

Imputation engine and settings: We will run multiple imputation in R with the ‘mitml’ package using ‘pan’ as the engine. Following recommended practice (e.g., Grund et al., 2018) and similar to de Haan et al. (2024), we will use a burn-in of 6,000 iterations, then draw m = 30 imputed datasets, each 200 iterations apart. Following recommended practice (Grund, Lüdtke, & Robitzsch, 2016, 2018) person-mean centering will be performed within each imputed dataset after imputation.

Diagnostics and sensitivity: We will inspect trace plots, the fraction of missing information, and within- vs. between-imputation variance to assess quality. If diagnostics indicate problems (e.g., poor convergence or very high fraction of missing information), we will increase m and/or the number of iterations and document any changes. For the body satisfaction imputation model, we will repeat respective analyses with complete cases only as a sensitivity check and compare the results to those from the multiply imputed data.

table.effect_size:
Appearance-ideal images featuring individuals who conform to beauty ideals have been shown in experimental studies to harm body image (de Valle et al., 2021). Specifically, de Valle et al. (2021)’s meta-analysis—a gender-inclusive synthesis in which participants were predominantly female (82.7%)—found that viewing appearance-ideal images on social media has an immediate, moderate negative impact on body image compared to (1) non-appearance control content (Hedges’ g = −0.61); and (2) other appearance-related images (Hedges’ g = −0.68). 

There is little meta-analytic literature on the impact of beauty-content or beauty-filters on body image. For beauty filters, experimental work shows that using a face-slimming filter on one's own image produces greater social comparison than viewing a neutral filter, with a large effect on state comparison outcomes (η²p = 0.20) in a controlled self-use paradigm (Schroeder & Behm-Morawitz, 2024). Given this is only a single study, we will take a more conservative approach and use the above mentioned meta-analysis as a reference point. 

For hypothesis 1, the effects of interest relate to the direct effect of the level 1 predictor variable (daily exposure time [in seconds] viewing content featuring at least one beauty filter on the level 1 outcome variance in state body satisfaction. Following Arend and Schäfer (2019), a moderate level-1 direct effect explains 9% of the outcome variance.
table.statistical_power:
The present study is powered for the primary hypothesis. Based on the information provided in the Dataset Used section, the analytic sample will consist of female adolescent participants who meet the inclusion criteria described above, including donating their TikTok data and completing the two-week EMA protocol. Extrapolating from the overall response rate to the end-of-day EMA response rate, eligible female participants have completed an average of 12 end-of-day EMA surveys. Because the data have a hierarchical structure, with repeated end-of-day EMA observations (Level 1) nested within individuals (Level 2), analyses will employ multilevel modeling to appropriately account for this dependency.

Daily-life assessments are nested within participants over time. Following best practices for power analysis in longitudinal daily-life studies with nested data, we base our power analysis on a comprehensive simulation study on two-level multilevel models which has been conducted by Arend and Schäfer (2019). Their simulation study suggests that the present study is powered to detect a moderate effect of the predictor daily exposure time (in seconds) viewing content featuring at least one muscular beauty filter on state body satisfaction at the following EMA prompt.
table.inference_criteria:
For Hypotheses 1, 2, 3, and 4 (directional predictions on body satisfaction scores and watch time), we will use one-sided p-values below .05 (one-tailed tests), consistent with the original document's treatment of its directional hypotheses. 

For Hypotheses 5 and 6 (non-directional), we will use two-sided p-values below .05 (two-tailed tests), since no directional prediction is specified. We will examine fixed-effect estimates, confidence intervals, random effects, ICCs, and explained variance for all models.
table.assumption_violation_model_non_convergen: We will perform non-parametric tests to assess robustness (see the section Reliability and Robustness Testing for details).
table.reliability_and_robustness_testing:
As a robustness analysis, we will rerun the analyses in which daily exposure time is the outcome (Hypotheses 3 and 4) using zero-inflated negative binomial regression if inspection of the outcome distribution indicates substantial non-normality, specifically pronounced right skew, overdispersion, and an excess of zero-valued observations that would make the assumptions of the primary linear mixed-effects model questionable. If the distribution of exposure time is approximately symmetric and the assumptions of the primary model are adequately met, this robustness analysis will not be conducted, as the zero-inflated negative binomial model would unnecessarily reduce statistical power. The robustness model will include the same fixed and random effects as the primary analyses but will model exposure time using a zero-inflated negative binomial distribution, which is more appropriate for overdispersed count-like outcomes with excess structural zeros.

1. Metadata extraction strategy

For each video in a participant's TikTok watch history, corresponding video metadata were obtained.

Beauty-filter classification: A video is classified as “beauty-filtered” if its metadata indicates use of at least one effect from the reference list below. We have constructed an a priori reference list of TikTok sticker effects that meet a working definition of “beauty filter”. On TikTok, a sticker effect is an augmented reality (AR) effect that users can apply to videos to modify or augment their appearance or surroundings. Beauty filters are defined as sticker effects that alter a user's facial or body appearance to conform more closely to idealized beauty standards, including changes such as skin smoothing, facial reshaping, makeup application, eye enlargement, lip enhancement, hair modification, or other cosmetic enhancements. This definition is consistent with prior experimental work examining beautifying and slimming filters (Schroeder & Behm-Morawitz, 2024).

To develop the reference list, we systematically identified candidate beauty filters using two complementary approaches. First, we labeled beauty filters based on their names having appearance-related keywords (e.g., “makeup”, “smooth”, “lipstick”, “lashes”, etc.). Second, MZ manually examined the 300 most frequently observed sticker effects in our dataset to identify additional appearance-altering effects that may not be captured through keyword labeling (e.g. “prettiest”, “cutest”).

Beauty content classification: A video was classified as beauty-related if it carried one or more of TikTok's official content diversification labels associated with beauty content. These platform-generated labels are assigned by TikTok and are presumed to be derived from multiple features of the video, such as its transcript, caption, and visual content. Each video could receive multiple labels. To identify the set of beauty-related labels, we used snowball sampling beginning with three seed labels: \"Beauty,\" \"Beauty and Style,\" and \"Beauty and Care.\" We then identified all labels that co-occurred with these seeds, yielding three additional unique labels: \"Outfit,\" \"Nail Art,\" and \"Hair.\" Accordingly, we defined beauty-related content as videos containing any of these six labels, which collectively accounted for approximately 12.0% (48,202 of 403,046) of all videos watched by eligible female participants.

2. Definitions and timing

Video watch duration estimation: For each video, we have the participant's start time of viewing but not a stop time, so watch duration must be inferred. We first construct gaps for each video, which is the time elapsed between when a participant starts watching one video and when they start the next. Because a gap can span time spent off the app, we adjust it based on session context (a session being a continuous block of active in-app usage): if the next video falls within the same session, the gap is the raw time between events; if the session ends before the next video starts, the gap is capped at the session's own end time, excluding the off-app interval; if no session covering the event exists to verify either case, the raw gap is retained but flagged as unverified; and if there is no next event at all recorded for that participant, the gap is left unbounded.

Then, we cross-check the gap with the video length. Where the video's own length is known (from the downloaded file), watch duration is defined as the shorter of the video's length and the session-aware gap. If the gap is shorter, it means the participant navigated away before the video finished, so the gap itself is the true watch time; if the gap is longer than the video's length (including an unbounded gap), there was enough time for the video to have played out fully, so we assume it did and count the full video length.

Where the video's own length is unknown, there is no independent value to check the gap against, so the gap itself must serve as the watch-time estimate. We accept it only after a trust check, applied in decreasing order of confidence: (1) if the following event is confirmed within the same session, the participant was continuously active in the app throughout, so the raw gap is used directly; (2) failing that, if a session log is available and shows the session ended before the next video started, only the time up to that session's recorded end is used, since that is the portion known to reflect active viewing; (3) failing that, the raw gap is accepted only if it does not exceed the participant's own median duration across their trusted videos, defined as videos with a known length whose next event was also confirmed within the same session, as a plausibility check in the absence of any session data; (4) if none of these conditions hold, including the case of no following event at all, we substitute a random draw from that same trusted distribution (the participant's own length-known, session-confirmed videos), rather than assuming the video was watched in full or leaving the duration unbounded.

Exposure calculation: Total exposure per day is defined as the sum of watch durations (in seconds) across all videos classified as containing at least one beauty filter or a beauty-related content diversification label for that day. This sum is restricted to videos watched between 4:00am and the moment of the end-of-day assessment on that day.

live_data_statements: Participants were substantially engaged with TikTok during the study period: they used the platform on a median of 14 of the 14 study days (mean 12.8, range 1-14), viewing on average 517 videos (median 484) and 107 minutes of video (median 91) per active day.

Moreover, the content we focus on here was narrowly defined: the visual criterion required a thin body in minimal or tight clothing, posing for the camera, whereas the experimental literature has often defined idealised content more broadly, for example as thinness alone. 37, 43, 44 The feeds our participants were actually served were far more heterogeneous in appearance content than our visual criterion could capture: content meeting it made up only 0.8 of roughly 91 watched minutes per day.
After participant and parental consent was obtained, participants completed a baseline survey collecting demographics, mental health, body image, and social media use.
After an invitation was sent, participants had three hours to complete the survey.

At baseline (day 0), participants and their parents provided consent, and participants completed questionnaires covering socio-demographics, the SDQ, the O2S3, and the IUS-C. Over the following 14 days, participants received three EMA prompts per day via m-Path-morning (start of day; within the two-hour window before school/work start), afternoon (within the two-hour window after school/work end), and evening (end of day; within the two-hour window before reported bedtime) -with three hours to respond to each invitation.

Per the preregistered unit-of-analysis criteria, participants were included if they (a) identified as female, (b) completed at least three valid EMA prompts assessing body satisfaction and (c) provided TikTok donation data with sufficient metadata to derive exposure variables.

Two participants were subsequently excluded because the TikTok data they donated covered a period entirely preceding their participation in the EMA study and therefore did not overlap with the EMA assessment window, precluding the derivation of time-varying exposure measures for any study day.
Participants were instructed: "Carefully read the following statements and select the option that best reflects the way you have felt since the last notification."

No participants were excluded on this basis; their available, overlapping days were retained and contribute to the analysis as usual, while non-overlapping days necessarily contain no derivable exposure data.

For state body satisfaction, two further types of missing data were expected: (1) participants did not fill in the EMA at the start/end of a given day; (2) participants filled in the EMA but skipped the state body satisfaction item.

text.text: Experimental studies show that viewing idealised bodies on social media can lower body satisfaction, but whether this extends to the content adolescents actually encounter is unknown, because studies of everyday exposure have relied on self-report rather than on what was actually viewed.
In an observational study, we combined TikTok data donation with a 14-day ecological momentary assessment in 66 female adolescents aged 14-18.

A locally run computer vision pipeline classified the visual content of 242,422 watched videos for thin and sexualised female bodies -coding the imagery itself rather than hashtags or captions -and metadata-based classifiers identified beauty-filter use and TikTok's own beauty-related content labels.
Content meeting the body criterion made up under one minute of roughly 91 watched minutes per day.
Across all three measures, daily exposure was not associated with end-of-day body satisfaction, within or between persons, nor was morning body satisfaction associated with subsequent exposure.
Everyday exposure to appearance ideals may be too sparse and too stable from day to day for day-level designs to detect any effect of it.

Social influence matters more in adolescence than at almost any other stage of life. 1 Today, much of that influence is mediated through screens.

text.text: Sensitivity to social influence is greatest in early to mid-adolescence, [2] [3] [4] [5] when young people feel a strong need to belong while still forming their identity and self-concept. 6, 7 What they absorb shapes how they see their own bodies: a healthy body image is associated with better psychological, emotional and social well-being, whereas negative body image is linked to low self-esteem, disordered eating and broader mental health difficulties. 8, 9 Adolescents encounter appearance-based norms constantly on social media -in the UK, nearly all adolescents report regular engagement with social media platforms, with usage now a routine component of daily life. 10, 11 TikTok is among the most heavily used platforms among adolescents. 10 Its short-video format delivers many separate items per session, and its main feed is chosen by a recommendation algorithm rather than by whom the user follows. 12, 13 Appearance-focused content now reaches millions of adolescents through algorithmically curated feeds: most 8-17-year-olds mainly scroll and watch rather than post, and much of what they see is selected for them rather than by them. 14 What adolescents encounter in these feeds has become a current policy question.

text.text: In 2025, the European Commission's guidelines under the Digital Services Act recommended that platforms prevent minors' repeated exposure to "content promoting unrealistic beauty standards" and switch off by default filters associated with negative effects on body image; 15 in September 2026, the Commission went further and proposed the EU Kids Act, which would turn these recommendations into binding obligations and bar under-13s from social media altogether. 16 Australia's minimum age of 16 for social media use took effect in December 2025, 17 and the United Kingdom has announced equivalent legislation for 2027. 18 Yet these measures rest on a thin evidence base, as shown by a narrative review commissioned by the UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. 19 Much of this traces back to measurement: Until recently, researchers had no way to observe what adolescents actually see in their feeds and no means of coding appearance content in video at scale; consequently, most evidence comes from laboratory exposure to static images or from self-reported exposure to appearance-based content.

text.text: Two developments make a different approach possible.

Data donation, grounded in the right to data portability under the UK GDPR, 20 lets young people export and share their own platform data, including full watch histories, for research; 21 and computer vision -artificial-intelligence models capable of recognising and labelling what is shown in an image or video frame -models can now classify appearance content in video at scale. 22 The present study combines both: We link the TikTok videos adolescent girls actually watched, captured through data donation and coded for appearance content with computer vision, to their body satisfaction reported three times daily over two weeks.

text.text: Adolescence is the formative period for body image. 23, 24 Culturally transmitted beauty standards in the West have proven to be remarkably hegemonic: despite greater variety in model body types, the predominant 'thin ideal' for women has remained largely unchanged over the past 50 years. 25 Two established frameworks explain how exposure to such ideal bodies becomes body dissatisfaction, and both suggest the current media environment may intensify the process.

text.text: The Tripartite Influence Model identifies peers, parents, and media as the primary sources of appearance norms, which act on body image through internalisation of the ideal and upward appearance comparison. [26] [27] [28] [29] Objectification Theory further holds that repeated exposure to sexually objectifying environments, including media, leads individuals to adopt an observer's perspective on their own bodies; this self-objectification manifests as habitual body surveillance and, in turn, body shame. 30 Internalisation of body ideals predicts body dissatisfaction across genders, but girls report more of it across countries and socioeconomic contexts. 31, 32 Social media use has been linked to higher body dissatisfaction, disordered eating symptoms, and self-objectification among adolescents and young adults. [33] [34] [35] [36] And exposure to idealised peer or celebrity content on Instagram and Facebook has been linked to increased appearancebased social comparison and negative mood. 37, 38 Yet at the population level, associations between aggregate social media use and adolescent well-being are typically small, heterogeneous across specifications, and inconsistent across individuals. [39] [40] [41] This apparent tension is informative rather than contradictory.

text.text: Time-based measures treat all screen time as equivalent, collapsing ideal appearance content together with content of no appearance relevance whatsoever; if the active ingredient is the depiction or promotion of idealised appearance, an undifferentiated exposure measure will necessarily attenuate the effect it is intended to detect.

Ideal appearance content is no longer only depicted but manufactured at scale: platforms offer beauty filters that users can apply to their own videos, and AI has made these filters ever more naturalistic.

Retouched images have been linked to lower state body satisfaction in adolescent girls. 42 Filtered, retouched and platform-labelled beauty content in short-form video is thus a further, increasingly prevalent channel for the same tripartite and objectification mechanisms.

text.text: Therefore, progress depends on measuring what adolescents are shown, objectively examining what they view, and linking this to their body satisfaction.

In the present study, sixty-six female adolescents donated their TikTok viewing histories and completed ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) three times a day for two weeks, including a daily body-satisfaction rating.
Linking the two sources allowed us to characterise the appearance content adolescents consumed over the course of a day and examine whether days with more of it are days with lower body satisfaction.

We measure appearance-focused exposure in three ways, each computed as the daily time (in seconds) a participant spent watching TikTok videos that (a) depict at least one thin and sexualised female body, coded by our computer vision pipeline from slim body stature, minimal clothing, and posing of body or face; (b) are tagged by the platform as using a beauty filter; or (c) carry one of TikTok's beauty-related content labels.
Measure (a) is derived from the visual video content; measures (b) and (c) are derived from video metadata .

These three measures capture distinct aspects of ideal appearance content: what actually is depicted in a given video, how a creator has modified their own appearance, and how the platform itself categorises content.
State body satisfaction assessed at the start of each day precedes the day's content exposure and end-of-day satisfaction follows it.
The study was preregistered in two separate and complementary registrations that share the same data sample, design, and differ only in the exposure measure.
The first preregistration focuses on visual TikTok video content and defines content exposure as visibility of thin and sexualised female bodies in video still images (https://osf.io/k7953).

Sixty-six adolescent girls rated how satisfied they felt with their body three times per day for two weeks, and then donated those two weeks' TikTok viewing data, comprising roughly 242,000 videos.

On an average day, the average adolescent girl watched 91 minutes of TikTok across roughly 500 videos, of which 0.8 minutes showed a thin and highly sexualised female body per our definition; beauty filters appeared in 1.7 minutes, and 12.5 minutes of video content carried one of TikTok's own beauty labels.
Body satisfaction, meanwhile, was more a stable characteristic than a daily state.

Girls differed considerably from one another in how satisfied they felt, but each girl varied little from day to day, and more than half never moved more than one point on the five-point scale in two weeks.
Under these conditions, the smallest within-person effect that this design could have detected was approximately 0.06 scale points per minute of exposure.

For this to be registered, a day with ten more minutes of such content than usual (before the evening or after the morning assessment, respectively) would have had to lower that evening's body satisfaction by roughly 0.6 points -close to one full step on the 5-point Likert scale -which almost never occurred.

Furthermore, if highly sexualised ideal appearance content would function by shaping what a female adolescent comes to regard as normal or desirable, as proposed by tripartite-influence and internalisation theory, then its effect will not be evident as a difference between, for example, Tuesday and Wednesday.
Rather, it would be evident in long-term differences in what girls have internalised from their feeds.

Moreover, the content we focus on here was narrowly defined: the visual criterion required a thin body in minimal or tight clothing, posing for the camera, whereas the experimental literature has often defined idealised content more broadly, for example as thinness alone. 37, 43, 44 The feeds our participants were actually served were far more heterogeneous in appearance content than our visual criterion could capture: content meeting it made up only 0.8 of roughly 91 watched minutes per day.

text.text: Furthermore, experiments present images in isolation, whereas in daily life the same imagery is embedded in rapid, continuous scrolling amid much other content.
Several limitations merit consideration when interpreting this null result.
Firstly, the design is observational, so it cannot establish or rule out a causal effect.
Secondly, an association could have been masked by unmeasured influences, such as the events of the day or the company in which videos were watched.

Bearing this in mind, the absence of a day-level association at this everyday dose does not contradict experimental evidence; rather, it suggests that laboratory exposure and contexts are not representative of daily-life exposure on social media and likely there is also co-use of other platforms (e.g., Instagram, Snapchat).
Finally, the present study investigated 66 UK female adolescents over 14 days; this design did not allow us to detect small effect nor to investigate long-term, low-dose exposure.
Thus, future research would benefit from investigating longer timescales in larger samples.

Our study implemented a novel design: social media data donation and a fully locally run computer vision pipeline -on-premises processing being an ethical requirement for material concerning minors -reconstructed 242,422 watched videos and approximately 5.6 million depicted person instances into per-event, time-stamped exposure, validated against blinded human review (Supplementary Section 3) and analysed under a preregistered plan with documented deviations, and complemented by two independently constructed, metadata-based classifiers of beauty-filter use and platform beauty labelling.

This yields an unprecedented, directly measured account of what adolescent girls are 'speed consuming' in daily life, at a granularity self-report cannot approach, and reveals the composition of algorithmically curated feeds from three complementary angles: highly sexualised ideal appearance content under one percent of viewing time, sexually suggestive posing characterising only about 1.1% of classified person instances, and beauty-related platform labels attached to roughly 14% of all watched time.
In conclusion, this study is the first to measure what adolescent female adolescents actually see on TikTok and to relate it to how they feel about their bodies on a daily basis.
Our findings show the difference between laboratory exposure and speed-consuming content in daily life.

The idealised content the field has studied in the laboratory makes up a sliver of everyday viewing, body satisfaction is close to a trait over two weeks, and on neither side is there enough day-to-day variation for a same-day effect to show, under any of three independent measures.
While the causal effects of highly sexualised ideal appearance content on viewers' body image are unclear, our study indicates a potential method for studying them.

text.text: After participant and parental consent was obtained, participants completed a baseline survey collecting demographics, mental health, body image, and social media use.

The baseline assessment included socio-demographic factors (age, gender, sexual orientation, nationality, socio-economic status), the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) 45 , the Online and Offline Social Sensitivity Scale (O2S3) 46 , and the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale for Children (IUS-C) 47 .

text.text: Participants also received a detailed introduction to the study procedure.
Participants then completed a 14-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA) protocol capturing daily fluctuations in body satisfaction, emotions, and related psychosocial variables.
Assessments were administered three times per day (morning, afternoon, evening) via m-Path.

EMA invitations were scheduled around each participant's reported availability at intake: the morning EMA within the two-hour window before their school start time, the afternoon EMA within the two-hour window after school ended, and the evening EMA within the two-hour window before their reported bedtime.
After an invitation was sent, participants had three hours to complete the survey.
The morning and evening assessments are classified as "start-of-day" and "end-of-day" respectively.
At the end of the EMA period, participants requested and downloaded their own TikTok data packages via their respective accounts.

Once their data donation packages were available, participants received a unique, personalised link to a secure data donation interface powered by Port, an open-source tool designed to facilitate privacy-preserving data donation.
Through this interface, participants could select and process their downloaded data locally on their devices without transferring the complete raw files to the researchers.

Port 48 then extracted predefined, research-relevant information from the participants' watch histories, including time-stamped records of the videos they had viewed, complete with unique identifiers.

The present study uses data collected from N = 358 adolescents aged 13-18 years recruited from six schools in Cambridge, Birmingham, London, Liverpool, and Manchester. 21 A subsample of 119 participants also provided TikTok data donation files and participated in the EMA component of the study, which involved completing three assessments per day over a two-week period in 2024.

text.text: Per the preregistered unit-of-analysis criteria, participants were included if they (a) identified as female, (b) completed at least three valid EMA prompts assessing body satisfaction and (c) provided TikTok donation data with sufficient metadata to derive exposure variables.

Because every EMA prompt (morning, afternoon, and evening) contained the state body satisfaction item, criterion (b) was implemented literally as at least three answered EMA prompts of any type (this and other resolutions of ambiguities in the preregistrations are listed in Supplementary Section 2, Table S5).

text.text: Sixty-eight female participants met all three criteria.

Two participants were subsequently excluded because the TikTok data they donated covered a period entirely preceding their participation in the EMA study and therefore did not overlap with the EMA assessment window, precluding the derivation of time-varying exposure measures for any study day.
The final analytic sample comprised N = 66 female adolescents, applied identically across all three exposure operationalisations reported below.

An a priori power analysis was conducted for the primary confirmatory hypothesis (H1), the within-person (Level 1) association between daily exposure to thin and sexualised female bodies on TikTok (in seconds) and subsequent state body satisfaction.

Given the hierarchical structure of the data, with repeated end-of-day EMA observations (Level 1) nested within participants (Level 2), a multilevel modelling approach that explicitly accounts for this dependency was required.

Based on the information available at the preregistration stage, an analytic sample of approximately 68 female participants was anticipated, each contributing on average 10 valid end-of-day EMA assessments across the two-week study period.
To inform the expected effect size, we drew on the experimental literature on exposure to appearance-ideal content.

In a meta-analysis of experimental studies, de Valle et al. 44 found that on the between-person level viewing appearance-ideal images on social media had an immediate, moderate negative effect on body image on the between person level relative to both non-appearance control content (Hedges' g = -0.61) and other appearance-related images (Hedges' g = -0.68).

Two further, non-preregistered daily exposure measures were derived using the identical watch-duration procedure (Supplementary Section 5) but different content classifiers (Methods, Beauty filter content classification and Beauty label content classification): daily time spent watching videos using at least one beauty filter, and daily time spent watching videos carrying at least one TikTok beauty-related content label.

To account for late bedtimes, a study "day" was defined as 04:00 on a calendar day until 03:59 the following day, as preregistered; this definition was applied identically across all three exposure measures.

Per the preregistration, three types of missing data were expected for TikTok content exposure (all hypotheses): (1) if participants did not use TikTok on a given day, they were coded as having had no content exposure; (2) if participants did use TikTok on a given day but some viewed videos were unavailable (e.g., deleted), each missed 1-second video still was assigned the average probability of containing a thin and sexualised body among the participant's other available video stills on that day; and (3) if participants did use TikTok on a given day but no videos were available, each missed video was assigned the average probability among the participant's available videos across the whole 14-day study period.

This content-probability substitution procedure is deliberately distinguished terminologically from the multiple imputation of body-satisfaction scores described below, since the two address different variables via different mechanisms; full implementation details are given in Supplementary Section 5.

An additional, unanticipated type of missing data occurred which is only considered in the beauty filter and beauty content preregistration: partially missing TikTok data for participants whose donation period did not fully overlap with the EMA assessment period.
In total, 16 of the 924 participant-days (1.7%) fell outside a participant's donation coverage.

No participants were excluded on this basis; their available, overlapping days were retained and contribute to the analysis as usual, while non-overlapping days necessarily contain no derivable exposure data.

Of 66 participants across the 14-day study period (924 possible participant-days), 754 participant-days (81.6%) had an evening EMA response recorded; on the remaining 170 participant-days (18.4%) the evening EMA was not answered, and end-of-day body satisfaction was multiply imputed as described below.

For state body satisfaction, two further types of missing data were expected: (1) participants did not fill in the EMA at the start/end of a given day; (2) participants filled in the EMA but skipped the state body satisfaction item.

Multiple imputation was conducted in R with the 'mitml' package.
The preregistration specified pan as the imputation engine, a burn-in of 6,000 iterations, and m = 30 imputed datasets drawn 200 iterations apart.
Two documented deviations from these settings were required.

First, household income -a person-level (Level-2) covariate in the imputation model -had missing values for 28 of 66 participants (42.4%), and the pan engine cannot impute Level-2 targets; imputation was therefore carried out through mitml's jomoImpute function.

A video is classified as "beauty-filtered" if its metadata indicates the use of at least one effect from the reference list below.
On TikTok, a sticker effect is an augmented reality effect that users can apply to videos to modify or augment their appearance or surroundings.

Beauty filters are defined as sticker effects that alter a user's facial or body appearance to conform more closely to idealised beauty standards, including changes such as skin smoothing, facial reshaping, makeup application, eye enlargement, lip enhancement, hair modification, or other cosmetic enhancements.

This definition is consistent with prior experimental work examining beautifying and slimming filters. 53 The beauty-filter reference list was built in two steps: candidate effects were identified from appearance-related keywords in their names (e.g., "makeup", "smooth", "lashes") and from a manual scan of effect names for appearance-altering effects the keywords missed (e.g., "prettiest"), giving the preregistered candidate list; every candidate was then reviewed by name, with unclear names looked up on the TikTok website, and effects that do something other than beautify (e.g., "Ugly Face") were excluded.

text.text: As per our preregistration, a video was classified as beauty-related if it had one or more of TikTok's official content diversification labels associated with beauty content.
Platformgenerated labels are assigned by TikTok and are presumed to be derived from multiple features of the video, such as its transcript, caption, and visual content.
Each video could receive multiple labels.
To identify the set of beauty-related labels, we used snowball sampling beginning with three seed labels: "Beauty," "Beauty and Style," and "Beauty and Care."
We then identified all labels that co-occurred with these seeds, yielding three additional unique labels: "Outfit," "Nail Art," and "Hair."

Accordingly, we defined beauty-related content as videos containing any of these six labels, which collectively accounted for 29,989 of 242,422 videos watched by eligible participants, or approximately 12.4%.

text.text: A zero-shot embedding classifier (Marqo-FashionSigLIP 60 ) scored each person-crop against 21 clothing categories and flagged 1,590,383 (55.0%) as plausibly revealing, deliberately favouring recall (distribution across the categories in Supplementary Table S7); a quality filter then removed incidental background persons, crops showing too little body below the shoulders, and blurred crops, retaining 1,050,974 (pass rates per criterion in Supplementary Table S8).
text.formatted: A zero-shot embedding classifier (Marqo-FashionSigLIP 60 ) scored each person-crop against 21 clothing categories and flagged 1,590,383 (55.0%) as plausibly revealing, deliberately favouring recall (distribution across the categories in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S7</ref>); a quality filter then removed incidental background persons, crops showing too little body below the shoulders, and blurred crops, retaining 1,050,974 (pass rates per criterion in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S8</ref>).

text.text: Every retained crop was put to four independent questions by the VLM, each answered yes, no or indeterminate: minimal or tight clothing (yes: 72,788; 6.9%), deliberate posing (618,987; 58.9%), sexually suggestive posing (11,702; 1.1%, with 15.8% indeterminate) and thin body build (565,675; 53.8%, with 38.2% indeterminate).
Prompts constrained the model to a single-word answer; indeterminate and refused responses (≤ 0.5%) never count as positive.

Combining the classifications, 32,441 crops (3.1% of the pool) met the confirmatory definition used throughout (minimal/tight clothing, posing, and thin body build), falling in 30,842 stills, 0.94% of all stills on screen; 4,729 crops (0.45%) met the preregistered definition, which requires sexually suggestive rather than any posing for the camera (Supplementary Section 3.7).
Validation.
Each step was checked against 1,000 randomly sampled stills by two independent, blinded reviewers.

Agreement with the classifier was 94.4% (human presence), 89.5% (female presence), 78.5% (clothing pre-filter), 71.3% (sexualised presentation) and 71.5% (thinness), with inter-reviewer κ between 0.65 and 0.84.

The preregistered 95% criterion was approached for the perceptual filters and not met for the interpretive judgements; because raw accuracy cannot distinguish under-from over-labelling, model error may be biased in either direction (Supplementary Sections 3.2-3.6).

An AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic; models Opus 5.5, Fable 5, Fable 5.1) was used during the development of the analysis code -including debugging, code structure, and iterating on prompt design for the content classification pipeline described above -and of the Python code used to produce the figures, under direct researcher supervision, with all outputs reviewed, tested, and approved by the authors before use.
The AI assistant was also used to improve portions of this manuscript for language, structure, and clarity, and for formatting, reference formatting, and typesetting.
